2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Not applicable / Can't tell: Non-cohort qualitative case study design; participant refusal rates or any drop-off across the two fieldwork phases (2015-2016 and 2016-2018) are not reported.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Not applicable (qualitative design): The study does not estimate quantitative causal effects, though it qualitatively contextualizes structural differences in class, topography, developer governance, and patronage networks between Izbet ElHaggana and New Cairo.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Moderate (qualitative institutional description): Legal and administrative arrangements—including the 2004 and 2006 presidential decrees corporatizing provincial utilities and tariff regulation, the 2008 governorate policy and 2013 Greater Cairo Water Company installation of legal metered pipes in Izbet ElHaggana, and New Urban Communities Authority / private developer governance in New Cairo—are traced via secondary literature, policy reports, and interviews rather than primary statutory or doctrinal coding.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate concern (Can't tell on data collection/analysis rigor): Data collection was asymmetric across sites (in-person visits and narrative walks in Izbet ElHaggana in 2015-2016 versus virtual/abroad interviews and the author's own lived experience for New Cairo in 2016-2018), and interview guides, recording/transcription, translation from Arabic, and qualitative coding procedures are unreported.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Qualitative experiential measurement: Water service outcomes (supply cutoffs, duration of shortages, yellowed water quality, storage/bribery expenses, and gehood zateya repair practices) rely on resident accounts, field photographs/observations, and local media reports rather than standardized hydraulic or water-quality measurements.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern (Can't tell): No interview protocol or systematic coding framework is reported to assess selective quotation across the 72 interviews, although the narrative candidly reports disconfirming nuances such as intra-community free-riding/conflict over informal pipe funds and developer-utility blame-shifting.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate-to-high concern (Can't tell on recruitment): While purposive selection of two contrasting Cairo settlements (informal Izbet ElHaggana vs. elite ElTagammo' ElKhames) fits the comparative theoretical aims, the paper provides no information on how the 72 interviewees were identified or recruited, site-specific sample counts, or how reliance on virtual interviews and personal familiarity in New Cairo shaped participant selection.

domain_ratings.justification: The author explicitly formulates two core research aims: interrogating how water infrastructure repair operates within hybrid configurations under formalization and privatization, and examining how informal everyday politics (gehood zateya) shape state-society relations across marginalized and elite areas of Cairo.

A qualitative methodology combining interviews, narrative walks, field observations, and archival research is well suited to investigating everyday socio-technical repair practices, informal patronage networks, and discursive narratives of infrastructural decay.

No qualitative analytical process is described (no information on coding, thematic derivation, triangulation mechanics across archival and interview sources, or handling of discrepant data), although findings are coherently structured and illustrated with direct participant quotes and counter-examples.

domain_ratings.justification: Empirical findings on post-formalization shortages and collective/networked repair in Izbet ElHaggana and fragmented developer/state governance, wasta, and decay narratives in New Cairo are clearly presented and explicitly synthesized against the theoretical framework in the Conclusion and Highlights.

domain_ratings.rating: Valuable contribution to urban water governance and legal-informality scholarship

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Wahby (2021) is a primary qualitative comparative case study investigating water shortages, infrastructural decay narratives, and everyday socio-technical repair practices (gehood zateya) across two settlements on Cairo's eastern desert periphery: the informal settlement of Izbet ElHaggana (following 2013 legal state pipeline installation) and the elite/middle-class district of ElTagammo' ElKhames in New Cairo. Assessed with the CASP Qualitative Checklist, the study has clear theoretical and empirical aims (Q1), an appropriate qualitative approach (Q2) and comparative two-site design (Q3), clearly articulated findings backed by illustrative vignettes (Q9), and high conceptual value for understanding why formalization and privatization do not displace informal water practices (Q10). However, methodological reporting is thin, yielding five 'Can't tell' ratings across recruitment strategy (Q4), data collection details and cross-site modality differences between in-person ElHaggana fieldwork and virtual/abroad New Cairo interviews (Q5), researcher positionality and use of personal experience in New Cairo (Q6), ethical review and informed consent beyond pseudonymization (Q7), and qualitative coding/analysis procedures (Q8). Overall methodological concern is therefore rated Moderate (5 Can't tell / 0 No items).
raw_response.overall_rating: Moderate concern (5 Can't tell / 0 No items)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Qualitative comparative case study (two-phase fieldwork comprising community visits, narrative walks, 72 in-person and virtual interviews, and archival research across two Cairo settlements)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Research aims and conceptual framing in Abstract (PDF p. 1) and Introduction/Literature Review (PDF pp. 2-6); legal-institutional water sector background in 'The political economy of Cairo's urban waters' (PDF pp. 6-8); study design, two-phase data collection, interview count (n=72), and site selection in 'Research methods and context' (PDF pp. 8-10); empirical findings in 'Results: Repair and decay in Haganna and Tagammo'' (PDF pp. 10-16); synthesis in 'Conclusion' and 'Highlights' (PDF pp. 16-19); anonymization and interviewee citations in 'Notes' 2-27 (PDF pp. 19-20).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The paper reports primary qualitative empirical research based on field visits, narrative walks, archival research, and 72 interviews across two urban case-study sites, with no quantitative dataset or statistical component; the CASP Qualitative Checklist is the protocol-specified appraisal instrument for primary qualitative studies.
